title: Applications of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

EL7-F-01.hint: To evaluate, replace \(t\) with the number of years. To find when a target is reached, divide to isolate the exponential, then take a logarithm of both sides.
slips: Rounding the growth factor before computing the power, which changes the answer.
Rounding down when the balance has not yet reached the target. Check the whole year in the model.

EL7-F-02.hint: Evaluate by substituting. To solve for \(t\), divide both sides by the starting amount, then write the result as a power of the base.
slips: Dividing the target by the base instead of by the starting amount.
Using the number of days as the exponent but forgetting to substitute in the model.

EL7-F-03.hint: The exponent \(t/\text{half-life}\) counts how many half-lives have passed. Evaluate by substituting; solve by dividing and matching the power of \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
slips: Using \(t\) as the exponent instead of \(t\) divided by the half-life.
Solving for the exponent and forgetting to multiply back by the half-life.

EL7-A-01.hint: For \(A=Pe^{rt}\), isolate \(e^{rt}\) and take the natural logarithm of both sides. \(\ln(e^{u})=u\).
slips: Taking the logarithm before isolating the exponential.
Forgetting that \(r\) is negative for decay, so \(t\) comes out positive only after dividing by a negative number.

items.stem: A savings account starts with $2,000 and earns 6% interest per year, compounded annually. The amount after \(t\) years is \(A(t) = 2000(1.06)^{t}\).

parts.q: Find the amount in the account after \(5\) years. Round to the nearest cent.
After how many years will the balance first reach $6,000? Give the exact solution, then round up to a whole year.
parts.a: Solve \(2000(1.06)^{t} = 6000\): \((1.06)^{t} = 3\), so \(t = \dfrac{\ln(3)}{\ln(1.06)} \approx 18.85\). The balance is below $6,000 after \(18\) years and above it after \(19\) years, so it first reaches $6,000 during year \(19\): \(19\) years.

items.stem: A sample of 200 grams of a radioactive substance has a half-life of 50 years. The amount remaining after \(t\) years is \(A(t) = 200\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/50}\).

parts.q: How much remains after \(100\) years?
After how many years will only 6.25 grams remain?
parts.a: Solve \(200\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/50} = 6.25\): divide by \(200\) to get \(\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/50} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{5}\). So \(t/50 = 5\) and \(t = 250\) years.

items.stem: The value of an investment grows continuously according to \(A(t) = 500e^{0.04t}\), where \(t\) is in years.

parts.q: Find \(A(10)\). Round to one decimal place.
When will the amount reach 1,500? Round to one decimal place.
parts.a: Solve \(500e^{0.04t} = 1500\): \(e^{0.04t} = 3\). Take the natural logarithm: \(0.04t = \ln(3)\), so \(t = \dfrac{\ln(3)}{0.04} \approx 27.5\) years.

items.stem: The mass of a decaying sample falls continuously according to \(A(t) = 500e^{-0.03t}\), where \(t\) is in years.

parts.q: Find \(A(10)\). Round to one decimal place.
When will the amount be half of the starting amount, 250? Round to one decimal place.
parts.a: Solve \(500e^{-0.03t} = 250\): \(e^{-0.03t} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Take the natural logarithm: \(-0.03t = \ln(\dfrac{1}{2})\), so \(t = \dfrac{\ln(\dfrac{1}{2})}{-0.03} \approx 23.1\) years.
